overview.title: 📖 Overview: When Exactly Is a Sin Offering 'Lost'?
overview.subtitle: Temurah 22a–22b
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: Reish Lakish states that a sin offering whose first year has passed is always left to graze, like an animal standing unreachable in a cemetery — seemingly contradicting the mishna's plain statement that it dies once the owner has atoned with a replacement. After several proposed readings are tested and rejected, Rava settles the matter by distinguishing single-disqualification cases (Reish Lakish's) from double-disqualification cases (lost AND blemished/aged). The Gemara then defines exactly what counts as 'lost' — distinguishing it from stolen or robbed, debating whether an animal merely out of sight (behind a door, mixed into a herd) qualifies, and probing whether blood already collected in a cup counts as 'atonement achieved' even before it's sprinkled. A new mishna then works through an elaborate chain of scenarios involving lost animals, lost money, and their replacements, closing with a dispute between Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and the Rabbis over what happens when both the original and its replacement turn up fit and available.

slides.title: 📅 Reconciling Reish Lakish With the Mishna
slides.subtitle: Multiple readings tested before Rava's final distinction
rows: Reish Lakish: year-passed animal ALWAYS grazes (regardless of atonement)
Seems flatly contradicted by the mishna's 'dies after atonement' ruling
Rabba: mishna's 'dies' clause is really about temporary-vs-permanent blemish timing
Rava: wrong verb used; doesn't explain why 'year-passed' is mentioned separately
The mishna's 'dies' cases involve TWO disqualifications at once (lost + blemished, or lost + year-passed); Reish Lakish addresses a single disqualification alone (never lost)

callout.label: Why both extra clauses were needed:
callout.text: Without both 'lost' variations spelled out, one might assume loss only matters for an aged-out animal (never fit anyway) or only for a blemished one (never fit at all) — each needed independent confirmation.

slides.title: 🔍 What Exactly Counts as 'Lost'?
slides.subtitle: Abaye's rule, and how visible an animal must be to NOT count as lost

nodes.content: 📜 Abaye's tradition: 'lost' triggers death — but NOT stolen, and NOT robbed. Only genuine loss counts
❓ How 'lost' must it be? Rabbi Oshaya: even ONE animal mixed into a large flock, or mixed with just one non-sacred animal, counts as lost
❓ Rabbi Yoḥanan: an animal simply standing 'behind the door' counts as lost
🤔 Does 'behind the door' mean ONLY there (unseen) counts, or does it mean EVEN there (where a turned head could spot it) counts — so anything less visible certainly does too?
⏳ תֵּיקוּ — left unresolved, along with a parallel dilemma about loss known to a distant stranger but not the owner or shepherd

callout.label: Underlying logic:
callout.text: An owner's hope that a lost (but not stolen/robbed) animal will be recovered is what keeps it in a 'graze' status rather than 'death' — theft removes that hope differently.

slides.title: 🩸 Does Blood in the Cup Count as Atonement Achieved?
slides.subtitle: Rav Pappa's dilemma about timing

steps.content: 1️⃣ A sin offering is lost; a replacement is designated, slaughtered, and its blood collected in a cup — but not yet sprinkled — when the original is found
2️⃣ Question: does blood 'standing ready to be sprinkled' count AS IF already sprinkled (meaning atonement is effectively achieved, so the original dies)?
3️⃣ Or: as long as it hasn't actually touched the altar, the situation is still 'lost at the time of designation' — so the original grazes
4️⃣ A second version of the dilemma: blood was split into TWO cups, and one cup is lost while the other is sprinkled — does the missing cup 'count' as present via the remaining one?

callout.label: Resolution:
callout.text: Both versions of this dilemma end in תֵּיקוּ — the precise moment atonement legally 'completes' remains genuinely unresolved.

slides.title: 💰 New Mishna: A Chain of Lost-and-Found Scenarios
slides.subtitle: Animal vs. money, lost vs. found, sacrificed vs. not — each combination has its own rule
rows: Animal lost, replacement SACRIFICED, then original found
Money lost, replacement animal SACRIFICED, then money found
Money is disposed of — cast into the Dead Sea
Money lost, replacement money designated, no purchase yet, then original money found
Buy a sin offering combining BOTH sums; leftover funds communal gifts
Animal lost, replacement blemished before sacrifice, then original found (also usable)
Sell the blemished one; combine proceeds with the other to buy one sin offering; leftover to communal gifts

callout.label: Guiding principle:
callout.text: Whenever no irreversible act (slaughter/sacrifice) has yet occurred, the law tries to salvage BOTH consecrated resources into one valid offering rather than wasting either.

slides.title: ⚖️ Both Animals Found Fit — Before Atonement
slides.subtitle: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi vs. the Rabbis, plus Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Shimon's addition

lines.speaker: Scenario
lines.text: One designates a sin offering; it's lost; he designates a replacement; before sacrificing it, the ORIGINAL is found — and both are unblemished and fit.

lines.speaker: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
lines.text: One is sacrificed as the sin offering; the OTHER must die — since being lost at all, even briefly, already disqualifies it from ever competing again.

lines.speaker: The Rabbis
lines.text: Not so — a sin offering is left to die ONLY if found AFTER atonement was achieved. Since atonement hasn't happened yet, either animal may still be sacrificed.

lines.speaker: Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Shimon
lines.text: Extends the logic further: even a sold, now-non-sacred former sin offering 'dies' in status (can't be un-sold) if the second animal is sacrificed before the FIRST is slaughtered for ordinary consumption — the sale doesn't erase its prior consecrated history.

callout.label: Underlying question:
callout.text: Does mere LOSS (even briefly, even before any atonement) permanently disqualify an animal, or does only actual completed atonement do so?

summary.principle: A sin offering is left to die only when TWO factors combine — being lost and unfit, or a loss that outlasts the owner's atonement — while the precise definitions of 'lost' and 'atonement achieved' (blood in a cup, an animal behind a door) remain genuinely contested or unresolved.

flowSteps.content: 📅 Reish Lakish (single disqualification: grazes) reconciled with the mishna (double disqualification: dies)
🔍 'Lost' (not stolen/robbed) defined loosely — even one animal mixed into a flock counts; visibility disputes left unresolved

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: only genuine, completed atonement — not mere loss or a not-yet-sprinkled offering — permanently disqualifies the original

quiz.q: How does Rava ultimately reconcile Reish Lakish's rule (a year-passed sin offering always grazes) with the mishna's statement that such an animal dies?
o: He says Reish Lakish is simply wrong
He distinguishes: the mishna's 'dies' cases involve TWO disqualifying factors at once (lost plus aged/blemished); Reish Lakish addresses an animal with only ONE factor (never lost)
He says the mishna doesn't really discuss year-passed offerings
He claims there is no contradiction to resolve
quiz.e: Rava's final resolution distinguishes double-disqualification cases (which the mishna addresses, leading to death) from Reish Lakish's single-disqualification case (aged out but never lost), which simply grazes.

quiz.q: According to Abaye's tradition, which situations trigger the 'dies' rule for a sin offering that becomes unavailable?
o: Any situation where the animal becomes unavailable, including theft or robbery
Only genuine LOSS — not theft, and not robbery
Only robbery, never simple loss
None of these situations matter
quiz.e: Abaye specifies that only a genuinely LOST sin offering (not stolen, not robbed) is subject to the 'graze until blemished, then possibly dies' framework — theft and robbery are treated differently.

quiz.q: What is Rav Pappa's key unresolved dilemma regarding blood collected in a cup but not yet sprinkled?
o: Whether the blood is ritually pure
Whether blood 'standing ready to be sprinkled' counts as already sprinkled (completing atonement) or whether atonement is only achieved once actually sprinkled
Whether the cup itself needs to be replaced
Whether the priest performing the sprinkling matters
quiz.e: Rav Pappa's dilemma, left as teiku, is whether blood collected and ready for sprinkling already counts as completed atonement (making the lost-then-found original animal 'die'), or whether only actual sprinkling completes atonement.

quiz.q: In the new mishna's scenario where money for a sin offering is lost, replacement money is designated, and no purchase has yet occurred when the original money is found, what is the ruling?
o: The original money is discarded into the Dead Sea
A sin offering is purchased using BOTH sums combined, with any leftover going to communal gift offerings
Only the replacement money may be used
Nothing may be purchased at all
quiz.e: Since no irreversible act (like slaughter) occurred, the mishna directs combining both sums to purchase one valid sin offering, with the remainder allocated to communal gift offerings.

quiz.q: In the dispute over two unblemished animals both found fit before atonement, what is the key difference between Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and the Rabbis?
o: They agree completely
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi holds any period of being lost permanently disqualifies the 'losing' animal (it must die); the Rabbis hold death applies only if found AFTER atonement was already achieved
The Rabbis are stricter than Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
Neither position allows either animal to be sacrificed
quiz.e: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi holds that mere loss (even briefly) permanently disqualifies the animal, while the Rabbis hold that only actual completed atonement (via sacrifice of the replacement) disqualifies the other — since atonement hasn't happened yet, either animal remains eligible.
